item.title: Church Pond
item.description: Church Pond is a little more than a mile off the Kangamagus Highway, but it feels much more remote. The usual route to the pond is from Camp Passaconaway via the Church Pond Loop Trail. While this used to be a loop, the east section of the trail is permanently closed, now making it an out-and-back route.
item.content:encoded:
Church Pond is a little more than a mile off the Kangamagus Highway, but it feels much more remote. The usual route to the pond is from Camp Passaconaway via the Church Pond Loop Trail. While this used to be a loop, the east section of the trail is permanently closed, now making it an out-and-back route.

After walking over bog bridges through a beautiful marsh, you arrive at a knoll on the east side of the pond. Follow one of the herd paths down to the shore for some great views especially to the southwest. Here is a dramatic view of Mt. Potash (left) rising on the other side of the Kangamagus. To the right of Mt. Potash is the valley of Sabbaday Brook with the Sleepers in the distance.

Swing to the right just a little and North Tripyramid comes into view.

Although it's definitely past peak foliage, the tamaracks are almost neon yellow this time of year.

Tamaracks are common in New Hampshire, but they almost never dominate the landscape. It's always a pleasant surprise to catch the tamarack show after most hardwoods have dropped their leaves.

item.title: Guinea Pond
item.description: Guinea Pond is located in the Sandwich Range Wilderness, just south of Sandwich Mountain. Black Mountain, a subpeak of Sandwich Mountain, looms over the pond.
item.content:encoded:
Guinea Pond is located in the Sandwich Range Wilderness, just south of Sandwich Mountain. Black Mountain, a subpeak of Sandwich Mountain, looms over the pond.

To the right of Black Mountain is Sandwich Dome, the true summit of Sandwich Mountain.

Zooming out a bit, you can see how truly massive Sandwich Mountain is. From this angle, it looks like an entire mountain range, but geographically speaking, it is a single mountain.

item.title: Alpine Garden
item.description: The Alpine Garden is an area above treeline on Mt. Washington's eastern slope between Tuckerman Ravine and Huntington Ravine. It's a place where several varieties of alpine plants produce flowers in June and into July. June 9 is early for the flowers of some varieties, but Lapland Rosebay (pink) and Diapensia (white) are blooming on the edge of Tuckerman Ravine.
item.content:encoded:
The Alpine Garden is an area above treeline on Mt. Washington's eastern slope between Tuckerman Ravine and Huntington Ravine. It's a place where several varieties of alpine plants produce flowers in June and into July. June 9 is early for the flowers of some varieties, but Lapland Rosebay (pink) and Diapensia (white) are blooming on the edge of Tuckerman Ravine.

The high winds of the Alpine Garden cause the stunted trees to twist into strange shapes or Krummholz.

Despite the difficult conditions, Alpine Azalea is thriving. This plant is in a little nook on the leeward side of a small rock.

And there are large patches of Diapensia and Lapland Rosebay everywhere you look.

item.title: Mt. Crawford
item.description: It's just over 3100 feet high, but Mt. Crawford has some of the best views in the White Mountains. Crawford Notch is just to the northwest.
item.content:encoded:
It's just over 3100 feet high, but Mt. Crawford has some of the best views in the White Mountains. Crawford Notch is just to the northwest.

Stairs Mountain is further up Davis Path to the northeast.

Mt. Washington is almost due north.

And that's just 90 degrees of the compass. Mt. Crawford has close to 360 degrees of views. It's well worth a visit.

item.title: Monadnock after a Nor'easter
item.description: Yesterday, a late season nor'easter dumped more than two feet of snow on the Monadnock region. The entire summit of Monadnock is under a blanket of white. If you look closely, you can see a lone hiker near the top of the mountain.
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday, a late season nor'easter dumped more than two feet of snow on the Monadnock region. The entire summit of Monadnock is under a blanket of white. If you look closely, you can see a lone hiker near the top of the mountain.

The high winds sculpted dramatic shapes in the snow.

The underlying rock emerges in places to remind us the snow is temporary. Spring is just around the corner. The melting snow will help the alpine plants thrive.
